author: Jessica Rish
title: Iowa City CSD faces public backlash amid financial woes. What to know - NewsBreak
text:
By Jessica Rish ,
12 hours ago
Amid ongoing financial concerns and public outcry, the Iowa City Community School District Board of Directors is planning to analyze administrative salaries and contracts.
The board discussed the framework for renewing, modifying, or terminating administrator contracts under Iowa Code Sections 279.23 and 279.24 during their regular meeting on Tuesday, April 14.
The discussion comes as the Iowa City Community School District tries to stabilize its finances after approving $7.5 million in spending cuts . The district also plans to borrow $35 million over the next two years to maintain cash flow to cover payroll and repay a $10 million interfund loan, as well as debt tied to facilities projects.
Attorney Kristy Latta said personnel contracts must be discussed in a closed session. The board needs to publicly vote to enter the closed session, then make final decisions in an open session.
More: Iowa City updates housing voucher program. How will it help residents?
The Iowa City community has demanded more accountability from district leadership, filling an hour of public comment at the start of Tuesday's meeting. A few suggested an overhaul of district leadership on the executive board, which would include superintendent Matt Degner.
“The situation facing the district is very serious…we passed the point of needing to change superintendents a long time ago, before it gets to making that decision, you need to start looking at an organizational audit,” said West High graduate John Fogarty, who has a child currently enrolled at Shimek Elementary. “…The organizational audit needs to examine all levels of administration...Not only is it beneficial in the long term, but it also gives your new superintendent a work plan of sorts to improve.”
Iowa City CSD faces public backlash over 'financial crisis' Other community members criticized Superintendent Degner's comments regarding the district’s partnership with the City of Coralville for its new recreation center and indoor competition pool . The district is pledging $14 million, despite its financial advisors revealing that the organization has only $1.5 million available each year for capital needs over the next two years.
Iowa Rep. Dave Jacoby, during a March 27 legislative session, asked how the ongoing budget crisis would impact capital projects, including the recreation center and its facilities master plan. Emily Campbell said Degner responded by saying the district was working on a way to fund the project. Campbell believes the ICCSD shouldn't be spending money on big projects.
“I want to be very clear, there should be no conversations with anyone about creative funding pathways for any capital projects right now. The district needs to stop and reassess its entire capital plan,” Campbell said. “… When FMP 2.3 was approved, there was no clear explanation or plan for how it would be funded, and financial advisors were kept in the dark. We’re now seeing the consequences of that. The district owes the public, our legislative partners, and the city of Coralville, honesty and transparency about where things stand.”
More: Iowa City CSD weighs school closures, $35M loan in latest budget talks
Former Iowa City mayor Matt Hayek said the school district's financial crisis is “self-inflicted” during Tuesday's meeting, the worst crisis in “our 170-year history,” caused “by serious mismanagement.”
Board members Jayne Finch, Mitch Lingo and Board President Ruthina Malone referenced the district’s financial situation as “a crisis” multiple times throughout Tuesday's meeting. Lingo says the district is in “an unprecedented financial crisis” due to overspending.
However, board member Charlie Eastham doesn’t see it that way and says, “Crisis is not an accurate description.”
“Frankly, the notion that we are in a crisis is not an accurate description of where we are financially in reality. I think we have difficulties and problems,” Eastham said. “I don’t think it is a crisis, and I think there are many people in the community that don’t think it’s a crisis, also.”
Jessica Rish is an entertainment, dining and education reporter for the Iowa City Press-Citizen. She can be reached at JRish@press-citizen.com or on X, formerly known as Twitter, at @rishjessica_
